introduction-from-code-to-customer.core: A CI/CD pipeline is an automated assembly line from commit to customer. Every change is built, tested and delivered the same way, quickly and repeatably, with no manual steps.

first_principles.problem: Manual builds and deploys are slow and inconsistent, and they depend on whoever happens to know the steps.
truths: Humans make mistakes on repetitive tasks.
Fast feedback catches bugs while they're cheap.
derivation: **CD**: automatically deliver passing builds to environments.
Break the work into **stages, jobs and steps**.

analogy.title: A car assembly line
analogy.story: Each station does one job in order, and every car gets the same inspections.
analogy.breaks: A pipeline is code too. It needs design, maintenance and security.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Minutes from commit to customer, every time the same way.

check.q: What's the difference between CI and CD?
check.a: CI builds and tests every change; CD automatically delivers or deploys passing changes.

the-hierarchy-stages-jobs-and-steps.core: Pipelines are hierarchical: stages run in order, jobs within a stage run in parallel on separate runners, and steps within a job run sequentially in a shared environment.

first_principles.problem: One monolithic script is slow (nothing runs in parallel), opaque and hard to rerun partially.
truths: Some work depends on earlier work.
Independent work can run in parallel.
derivation: **Job**: an isolated unit on its own runner; parallel within its stage.
**Step**: a command within a job, sharing its filesystem.

analogy.title: A restaurant service
analogy.story: Courses (stages) come in order; several cooks (jobs) prepare dishes for the same course at once; each cook follows recipe steps.
analogy.breaks: Jobs don't share files. You must pass artifacts explicitly.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: unit and lint run simultaneously after build.

check.q: Do two jobs share a filesystem?
check.a: No. Each job runs on its own runner, so files must be passed as artifacts.

artifact-management-passing-the-baton.core: Artifacts are the outputs of one stage (binaries, images, reports) saved and handed to later stages. Build once and promote the same artifact everywhere, so what you tested is what you deploy.

first_principles.problem: Rebuilding in each stage means production runs a binary that was never actually tested.
derivation: **Upload** the build output as an artifact.
Version and **store** release artifacts in a registry.

analogy.title: Passing the baton in a relay
analogy.story: The same baton travels the whole race; you don't make a new one at each hand-off.
analogy.breaks: Pipeline artifacts expire. Long-term releases belong in an artifact registry.

example.title: Build once, test and deploy the same JAR

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: The tested bits are exactly the deployed bits.

check.a: So the artifact you tested is byte-for-byte the one that reaches production.

caching-speeding-up-the-process.core: Caches store reusable inputs (dependencies, build caches) between runs to save time, keyed on something like a lockfile hash. Artifacts pass required outputs within a run. If a cache is missing, the job is just slower.

first_principles.problem: Every run re-downloads 800 MB of dependencies, adding minutes to every pipeline.
truths: A cache should be optional; correctness can't depend on it.
derivation: Never rely on a cache for **correctness**.

analogy.title: Keeping pantry staples
analogy.story: You don't buy flour for every cake; you restock only when the recipe changes.
analogy.breaks: Poisoned or stale caches cause weird bugs, so key them carefully and allow clearing.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Install drops from 3 minutes to 15 seconds on a hit.

code.text:
- uses: actions/cache@v4
  with:
    path: ~/.npm
    key: npm-${{ hashFiles('package-lock.json') }}
    restore-keys: npm-

check.q: What's the key difference between a cache and an artifact?
check.a: A cache is an optional speed-up; an artifact is a required output passed between jobs.

runners-the-engine-room.core: The CI platform only coordinates. Runners (agents) are the machines that execute jobs. Hosted runners are convenient; self-hosted ones give control, special hardware and network access, but you must secure and scale them.

first_principles.problem: Jobs need GPUs, private network access or lots of capacity that hosted runners don't provide, and self-hosted runners can be a security risk.
truths: Runners execute untrusted code from PRs.
derivation: **Self-hosted**: custom hardware and network, but you maintain them.

analogy.title: A dispatch office and its drivers
analogy.story: The office (platform) assigns deliveries; drivers (runners) actually do them. Some deliveries need special trucks.
analogy.breaks: Persistent self-hosted runners accumulate state and can be compromised by malicious PRs.

example.title: Adding GPU tests
flow: Ephemeral pod per job via ARC

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Special hardware with no leftover state.

example.outcome: the right compute for each job, securely.

check.a: Each job gets a clean machine, so no state or compromise carries over between jobs.
